doc.title: Joe Muranyi interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 11, 2007

title: Armstrong never lost his fire; Roy Eldridge, Zutty Singleton and Louis as friend
summary: Armstrong kept his fire; he played with Roy Eldridge and Armstrong simultaneously, reunited Zutty and Louis, and describes Louis's warmth.

story.theme_name: Working with and around Louis Armstrong
story.community_name: Playing with and around Louis Armstrong

blocks.x: Oh that right. That’s it. Jesus, isn’t that terrible. Years ago I was so sharp and now I forget that sort of thing. But anyhow the point is he never lost it, Louis Armstrong. And now this gets into the definition very much, you made a good point there. You say well “Hello Dolly” time is, you know, it’s certainly not as interesting as “Struttin’ With Some Barbecue” or “Potato Head Blues,” you know, naked creativity. The situation was completely different. But he never lost his fire. He always showed something. And what happens is like Roy Eldridge. I ended up playing at Ryan’s with Roy Eldridge. I played

with Roy for ten, eleven years. And at the same time I was playing with Louis Armstrong. Would you believe that? Me, the immigrant’s son? Ofay Joe? You know? And I got involved between them with the deepest S-H-I-T you know. And Zutty Singleton was involved in it you know. I got Zutty and Louis Armstrong together when Zutty had a stroke. I told Louis it’s all — and remember he went to see Zutty and they hadn’t been together for years and years you know. And it was like Pops was putting down — oh he can’t play drums with us, etcetera. And he went to visit Zutty in the Woodburn Hotel over here. And you know Zutty had a lot of fans, Ahmet Ertegun liked him and Ahmet, you know he just died. And he said, “if you need anything” he said, “you call me, don’t call your white friends” your rich white friends you know. There’s a marvelous story about, and you know Louis, he was a saint. And it was the biggest thing in my life, and I’m going to get teary, I’m near to. He was a wonderful guy. And he could be a bastard and he could be, oh a terrible, he could hurt you so badly and nobody in the world could do that. But anyhow the point is I liked him and he liked me. And the thing is I’ve never yet, and you know I’ve talked to people for a hundred years, “you ever see Louis?” And you know you hear the most interesting things you know. And most everybody that got to know him or knew him a little, Louis was his best friend. You know Louis had this quality, Louis as he called himself, had this quality, he was very gregarious and very good with people and he liked people, and he would really go out of his way and you know you would think well the big man doesn’t have time for that, but he did make time. And a lot of people thought that he was a much better friend than he was. Not that he wasn’t a friend but he had this quality that he exuded.
Sure. You felt like he was —
So and I include myself. So when I say this, maybe I’m from — but he was awfully nice to me.
